Many moons ago in 2003 I stumbled upon a trailer for a game called S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Oblivion Lost. After watching said trailer, I quickly became obsessed with the game. I wanted to learn everything I could about it. I searched high and low across the internet for every bit of information I could uncover. Eventually I found the developers forums (GSC) and that became my second home while I awaited its release. 

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oqQt-C6KB_8&list=PLAl2CYaVBm6BBV1PbLqoVTbqchC9tHiaz&index=15&t=67s

I remember at the time I was playing Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind, With it I fell in love with non-linear open world 1st/3rd person games with RPG elements and how much I could get immersed in virtual worlds. I am all for fantasy settings don't get me wrong, but there is nothing more terrifying than reality. (With a spin of fiction of course, alternate reality if you will) The abandoned urban/industrial locations in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. were more my cup of tea. That in itself made me very excited to play it. I couldn't wait to get lost in its world. 

While I waited though I researched about the nuclear disaster at Chernobyl in April 1986, it was mixed emotions for me. I was sad/amazed/intrigued. Sad for all of those people who lost their lives because of this. Nothing but respect for the liquidators and anyone involved in the initial cleanup. Those people are heroes and deserve nothing less. Amazed that this game had some real history in its background story. Even if it is incredibly embellished (mutants, anomalies, artifacts etc etc.), you have to admit it makes for an interesting premise to a story. Finally, Intrigued on what these game developers had in store for the players to experience, without making a mockery of those who had lost their lives in this tragedy. The game also borrows elements from "Roadside Picnic" by Boris and Arkady Strugatsky and the 1979  Andrei Tarkovsky film "Stalker". If you haven't heard or checked them out yet, they are most definitely worth it. Masterpieces in their own right.

Well turns out it was a long wait lol, game finally arrived in March 2007. It was no longer Oblivion Lost, it was now called Shadow of Chernobyl. Which was a welcomed change imo, what was not a welcomed change was the amount of content/features that were removed from the game. Vehicles, locations/maps made smaller and simpler, monsters/mutants, superior lighting from old alpha builds among many other things had been removed it was rather disappointing to say the least. The survival aspect of the game took a huge hit, leaving many in the community confused as to what happened during development. GSC Game World regardless of all the missing features still delivered a good game and it was well received by critics as well. 

The game at release had performance issues and bugs that required some official patches + plus community fixes. Once that happened it was clear that S.T.A.L.K.E.R. - Shadow of Chernobyl was a game ahead of its time. In a league all its own and a true gem in the PC gaming world. The atmosphere takes front row seat in this game it is almost like another character in the game. Such believable atmosphere it is downright amazing, it keeps you on the edge of your chair as you play. 

[u]Pros[/u]:
- Incredible atmosphere!
- Impressive use of lighting and shadows, 
- Cloud shadows that shift as day/night cycles progress. 
- None stylized (photo based) textures (realism), Replicating the rust and decay feel.
- Great cut-scenes that hold up even by today's standards. 
- Plenty of side quests 
- Exploring is encouraged to find secret stashes scattered throughout the world to find loot, weapons, ammo, suits and artifacts. Artifacts can be placed on your belt to grant the player abilities like resistance to radiation, increase weight limit etc. Some interesting combinations that can be made with the multitude of artifacts available in the game. 
- The games AI can be quite challenging because they adapt/react/flank/take cover depending on your approach. This adds to the games replayability immensely, if its one thing I have learned playing this game is that when it comes to killing the AI is that no playthrough is ever the same. Never. They are very unpredictable lets put it that way.
- Trading system with merchants and other friendly AI characters
- "The Zone" is alive even when you are not in the same vicinity, AI will be fighting mutants and/or other factions (Bandits, Duty, Freedom, Loners, Military, Mercs, Ecologists & Monolith) All fight among themselves.

Besides all the bells and whistles the story is incredibly engaging and keeps you interested throughout. Without too many spoilers (I am sure most people reading this have already played this but still) You play as "Marked One" an amnesiac trying to retrace his steps, he is then set on a mission to the heart of "The Zone" (term used to refer to the 30 kilometer Chernobyl Exclusion Zone, established after the accident.) to find a target and their whereabouts. Game also has multiple endings depending on the choices made by the player, 7 in total.

[U]Cons[/U]:
- Lots of "fetch" side quests (Surprise? lol)
- AI that can sometimes see you from "miles" away (vanilla)
- Some quest giving characters can die. (vanilla)

Just a heads up. Nothing game breaking but worth noting. Just like all games, it's not perfect.

Pros:
1-It doesn't feel repetative, and it's hardly scripted. Random events and enemies, as well as a developed "life cycle" for NPCs, makes the world feel alive and dangerous. 

2-Edit: Gunfights are properly deadly, and almost anything dies in 1 headshot. Spray and pray and run and gun doesn't work. You need to get low, take cover, and aim center mass until you have an accurate gun.

3-Mutants are uncommon and appropriately dangerous, if not outright lethal. Also pretty god damn scary since you find them in the lease pleasant or visible places.

4-Anamolies are plenty, making you constantly vigilent, and range from "ow that hurt" to "bloody meat chunks." They add a bit of puzzle/navigation type play now and again.

5- Edit: After finishing the game, I can safely say I found myself using almost every rifle for some time, 3 shotguns, 2 sniper rifles, half the pistols, at least 5 armors, and even a god damn RPG-7u. In the words of Gears, variety is the spice of death.

6-Immersion is great, with the zones ambience broken only be sporadically and properly placed fleeting notes of music. Turn of hud for extra immersion stalker. You will get scared sometimes, this is horror done well.

7-It unintentionally funny now and again.

8-The mod community is great, and there are plenty of great mods to not only fix some if the base games issues (if you can call them that) but also update the graphics for those who want a more modern looking game (Complete mod is a great place to begin.)

Neutral points:
1-Base game lacks the function of repairing weapon and armor. If you're like me, you will hate this. If you're not like me, you won't mind, you might actually like this as it may add to the immersion of having your weapons degree under constant use. I see it as if you get a cool and powerfull special weapon, you feel not inclined to use it in fear of degrading its durability. Easily cured with mod.

2-At the great time of 2007, surround sound wasn't exactly on point. This game very much has sound coming evenly at once from both left and right speaker, with no directionality. Not very useful for finding enemies, so much as knowing that they are indeed nearby enough. Not gamebreaking, but I normally use audio for that purpose in shooters.

3-Edit; Story is so-so. It feels a bit strung out since between getting missions and completing them, you don't get too much narration or explaining done to you until you literally beat (or almost) beat the game. The real story imo is the one you make while stalking.

Cons:
1-There are a few points in the game that are still bugged, since they never got fixed. One of them happend to be a NPC escort mission I had to redo for 3 hours to succeed and not get a bug/break in the mission(though it wasn't tied to main story progression, still annoying as hell). Needless to say, I don't believe any bugs are gamebreaking or impeed progression, but the game might work against you in a few occurences.

2-tldr; if you can't be arsed to read point 3 since it's technical babble; moding the graphics to be better will take a toll on your PC. Recommended you do so at your own risk and with a higher end rig.

3-Complete mod. Now, while it is a fully functional, non-game breaking mod that adds (in my opinion) several desired game features like a more modern look, there is one issue; optimization. Stalker doesn't run well on multiple cores and this compounds the mod; it actually took my first core hostage and ran it to 100% bottlenecking (I've got an OC'd i7-3770k 4.5Ghz processor, so not a weak CPU). This immense load is only in the modded game, since the texture overhaul is a big one. Now, disabling the first core and setting priority for the game engine to high distributes the load well among you other cores, but makes the GPU take a heavy brunt of it due to, again, optimization (I've had the game reach 70% on a few parts for my Gigabyte GTX 1080, no small feat for 2007 release). Stuttering is also an issue, but by setting the alife setting (go to steam games in your PC files, find stalker SoC, then just type alife in the searchbar) to be roughly 900, it prevent loading of things every time you move a short distance.

Verdict:
We thought the slavs only brought us the great joy of quality in the Witcher 3. We were wrong, since they've been actually doing it all the way back in 2007 with the S.T.A.L.K.E.R series.

With Stalker 2 here now, writing a quick review for the OG feels necessary:


Shadow of Chernobyl is the "truest" of the first three games. Its all about the mystery, allure and quite horrific nature of the zone. While the later games would try and explore the bright side of the zone, SoC just oozes darkness, danger, radioactivity, violence and flesh ripping anomalies.

The gunplay can vary in quality. Its definitely a frustrating experience with the starter guns and especially if they have non-green durability. Mid and high tier weaponry is rewarding and second only to CoP. 

The story is serviceable. Its not grandiose and altough it follows a protagonist, its definitely world-centered. Its pacing is strange but personally in a good way, keeping enough details in the dark to imagine crazy stuff.

The world itself is a 10/10, no other game in the series has this much detail and evident effort visible in its maps. Textures are raw and cold, the skyboxes are breathakingly overcast, the CNPP looks as mighty as the game hypes you up. Sound design is so iconic even S2, years later, reuses most effects in it.

Game pacing is decent. The beggining can be very slow, the midgame as long as you want, and the endgame is a race to the finish line, depending which ending you get. The second half of the experience is well directed, never overstaying its welcome (except for the true ending, a real ammo-dump).

Personally, SoC is very different to its succesors in tone, in the jankiness of the xray engine, the quality all around. It really feels like an anomaly, a forbidden sight just barely keeping it, always threatening you with a crash, but at least in my case only 2 happened. If you dont know which of the three games you want to try, Shadow of Chernobyl is the CORRECT answer.

In one sentence this is "An equipment based RPG shooter, with a creepy atmosphere in a post Soviet apocalyptic environment".

The game has a bad opening but if you can get past the first 30 ish minutes it becomes a tense shooter with great moments, some that were scary but not in a cheap way.

If anyone reads this here are some tips to get started.
1. Play on veteran or master difficulty- on easy mode all the enemies are bullet sponges but on hard they deal more/take more. Much better way to play plus you'll learn quickly why cover and ammo conservation matter.
2. the pistols in the beginning suck. take it slow until you get better weapons.
3. You dont need to take every gun or thing and sell it as money is not that hard to grind. 
4. Be smart about what you are carrying. You can store spare equipment in blue chests near traders ( of which there are few in the game) but try to be aware of how much you are carrying.
5.Flashlight is bound to "L", night vision ( once you get armor that has it) is set to "N". Change ammo type is set to "Y". There is also a keybind to change fire mode from semi auto to single shot, and also for some rifles from bullets to the attached grenade launcher.
6. There is no thirst mechanic but there is hunger- eat some food every day to be healthy. You can drink energy drinks to restore stamina though.
7. There is no way (even with console commands) to bring people back to life when dead. If they die, thats how life is in the zone.
8. Use F6 to quick save and F7 to quick load. Use this often. Also make occasional saves as the game can crash, seemingly randomly.
9. There are no 1 of a kind artifacts, but some are incredibly rare.
10. Explore the environment, there is a lot hiding for you to find.

This game is a mess and runs on the most classic example of a sketchy and unstable Eastern European game engine. Not only is the game old, but it feels old, looks old, plays old, and you're probably going to want an update on your tetanus shot. The combat is so clunky, that you're arguably more of a danger to yourself than most of the AI is to you. The AI itself is either running 300iq plays on you and your tactical clown shoes, or it's clipping on ground clutter objects. Every gun that you pick up will be nearly destroyed and every gun you carry with you will suffer the same atrophy. You will be in a combat situation where you will be very near death and your gun is going to jam on you, just as you really need it. You will encounter every kind of game breaking, mischevious, and murderous bug possible. All of those times in those other survival horror games where you thought you were low on ammunition have nothing on this. You're going to be down to a magazine of .556 and several thousand rounds of 9mm. Then you're going to realize that 9mm doesn't really count as bullets. You're going to be a kilometer underground fighting the infinite horrors of the slavic imagination and most worried about starving to death because monsters don't carry bread. You're going to be carrying out an assassination contract on someone one map distance away and they're going to be killed and stripped by bandits before you even get there. In five years you'll be driving through the bad part of town, admiring all of the post-industrial ruin with a painful nostalgic feeling in your chest because nothing will ever compare to your first time booting up S.T.A.L.K.E.R and walking into the zone.
This isn't a game. This is an experience. This is a feast for the eyes and a dagger to the heart. True love exists and she doesn't love you back. welcome to the zone.

In closing: I can't rate this game out of 10, because a numeric value does not come close to explaining what you're going to see here. You may have experienced environmental immersion in a video game, but this goes beyond that. There is a supernatural aspect to the sandbox in this game that I will not be able to communicate to you. You will just have to see it for yourself.

Also: Call of Chernobyl is a mod that combines the areas of all three stalker games into a single game, presented as a sandbox. It is unstable and pretty sketchy to run with a lot of mobs, but It's a good way to follow up a play-through of this.

After 11 years of owning this game and it sitting in my library,  I finally decided to sit down and play all the games before S.T.A.L.K.E.R 2 releases (and before I actually try to play the Anomaly mod pack, as intended by the devs). And after all this time & attempts at getting into it... I finally get it. This is absolutely one of the best Survival FPS games ever created.
 
It does what the 3D fallout games do but better (gameplay, story, environments, music, characters/factions). I'd say the main difference is that the world feels so lively compared to Fallout. It feels like the world continues without you when you're done playing but thats where those comparisons end. Mostly because I wouldn't call it "Post-Apocalyptic" as the world as we know it outside of the Zone exists still (spoiler alert, Chernobyl exists IRL! Wow!). There are no real perk/RPG elements to the game besides stats for your character, either. If you want to get technical - the artifacts you collect can be considered perks in a sense, but they really only enhance stats but have a lot of tradeoffs. 

The atmosphere of this game is literally unmatched, the closest I have felt to this recently is Tarkov. Which unsurprisingly, after playing this game it made me realize that Tarkov takes a lot of mechanics from this game. That isn't meant to be a negative either, in fact playing Tarkov beforehand made this game much easier for me. 

I am going to assume if you're reading the reviews/interested you already know how this game plays. And instead of talking indepth about it and and sounding like a wiki - I'd like to share some tips:

The vanilla experience like many fans say is fine and should not need gameplay mods on your first playthrough, honestly, 
I don't think graphical mods are really needed either. However I would STRONGLY suggest you install ZRP. It includes some QoL features and bug fixes, I only really suggest this because the game can and after a certain point WILL crash on you, the ZRP mod fixes those issues for the most part. 

Find things feel weird and awkward (ex 'X' being the run key, whatever the hell the weapon fire mode button is, crouching) Rebind. Your. Keys. ESPECIALLY SAVE/LOAD! I would suggest binding load further away from the save key. 

Speaking of saving, I highly suggest saving before any possible encounter or level switch. Later in the game, saving before level switches will save you time if you get the occasional loading crash. If using ZRP you can press ESC and press S it will create a lvl named save. 
--
(The rest are up to personal preference but this is how I enjoyed the game)
Use whatever difficulty you want. I've read many arguments about this before playing the game and came to the conclusion it doesn't matter that much and chose master anyway because I enjoy dying over and over in video games.

Turn off the crosshair. At range you will ADS/Use a scope and CQC you will probably be point firing anyway. It gets in the way and kinda takes away from the immersion, the hud is fine.

Rebinds I did were: Sprint as Shift, Crouch as C, Low Crouch as Ctrl, and fire mode as B. Save game as F5 and Load on Num *

Equipment load matters. Carry like 300 bullets for your guns and 15x bandages and antidotes, 3-4x medkits of each and maybe 5x of 2 sets of grenades. Carry guns of different bullet types as well, you'll find that newer weapons will have a low amount of ammo starting out so keep a backup. 

I didn't do this but figured it'd be helpful: If you would like to not be shot at later in the game when backtracking to a certain area - stay neutral (loner) and try not to fight the factions. Bad shit happens in one or two areas if you turn on a certain side. 
---
I cant list everything here, and I've only completed 2 of the multiple endings. But the community has way more tips/fixes/workarounds if you encounter any other issues/questions on the forums/subreddit/internet/google.com.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R is a really great game, I'd personally recommend getting all three if you can afford it.  While STALKER may not have the best graphics or story, it has some really engaging gameplay and moments, such as creeping your way through abandoned buildings and nuclear power plants we've all come to grow fond of from other games and movies.  That being said, this is an old game, and please consider that whilst purchasing and playing.  Some parts of the game have not  aged particularly well, and if you are not a fan of older games or just not an experienced player it may come off as unfairly hard(and due to bugs, it sometimes may be), however there are a lot of mods you can use on this game to enhance this one of a kind experience, or if you prefer vanilla there is still quite a lot to get out of this game.  

One tip for newbies, play on the hardest difficulty.  While that may sound insane for a game with such a reputation for challenging gameplay, it will make your experience much better.  STALKER manages hits in an "interesting" way.  Unlike most shooters where you just point your gun and it'll shoot, STALKER has a couple things that affect your aim, both scoped and hipfiring.  The first main thing is your movement and stance, while holding shift to walk slower, you will aim better.  Additionally, if you crouch while aiming, you'll improve a lot, and if you crouch and hold shift to go even slower, you'll be pinpoint accurate at almost all ranges, depending on your weapon.  The second thing that affects your aim, is the difficulty.  On lower difficulties, enemies will hit less of their shots, however, so will you.  Because the enemies in STALKER are quite tanky, and ammo is a precious resource, you're gonna want to be going for headshots.  Bumping up the difficulty and taking it slow will make the game much more enjoyable than running and gunning, trust me.

Tips for fighting human enemies: Keep calm, and fire in short, controlled bursts. Aim for the head, and avoid fighting multiple people at once.

Tips for fighting monsters: While you're busy screaming and covering your eyes, continuously move your mouse around while firing indiscriminately to increase your chances of survival.

[h1] What to Expect from an Early 2000s Classic [/h1]

I heard a lot of hype about STALKER and I'm sure you have too given the massive cult following of the game. When I first got it, I expected something similar to Fallout, but more hardcore. What I got was a good game with a few unexpected twists. Here is an overview of some of the things you need to know before you buy.

[h2] The Setting [/h2]

STALKER takes place within The Zone, a post-double-disaster Chernobyl. The landscape is barren, inhospitable, and generally depressing. There is little to look at save for some trees, roads, destroyed buildings, and rubble. The world is somewhat sparse and [b] all travel is done on foot, there is no fast travel in this game. [/b]

The landscape is populated entirely by men and monsters. There aren't any misc items such that you would find in a game like Skyrim or Fallout. There are no containers to open, mainly there are just boxes to smash to get some ammo drops or a medkit. There are a total of 3 or so food items (so far as I can tell). So, don't expect a ton of loot to find.

Also, and this is important, [b] the map is NOT open world, it's a vast landscape that is divided into sections. When you travel from section to section, you have to wait through a loading screen. [/b]

The map is dotted by "anomalies." these are essentially pockets of areas that you don't want to be in. Some crush you instantly, some zap you with electricity, some are made of acid, some explode. You can see these all over the world as you walk down the road. These anomalies cause "artifacts" to spawn, which are essentially shiny rocks that give you stat boosts and that you can sell for a good chunk of change. They give you effects like +3 bulletproofing and -5 radiation, etc.

Generally, there isn't a whole lot to explore or look at in this game world. However, where the game shines is the atmosphere. It's depressing and quite frightening at times. The sound design is exceptional, very immersive and captivating. You will be unnerved at times, I guarantee it.

[h2] The Missions [/h2]

Now, we have to talk about the missions. I'm still in the process of working through the main story, but generally missions are given via dialogue with NPCs. These are provided in the style of Morrowind, wherein some dialogue is voice acted, but most is simply reading a text box. 

The vast majority of missions seem to be fetch or kill quests. Go here, kill this guy, get this document, etc. There isn't a whole lot of variety or creativity there.

[h2] The Gunplay [/h2]

Another important thing to point out is the gunplay. The battles in this game can be lengthy due to most enemies being bullet sponges. I mean, you can shoot an entire clip into an enemy at point blank range and the guy will still be alive. On top of this, enemies appear to respawn after a certain period of time. I had an instance where I had to defend an area from a wave of bandit. Once I killed the wave and got the mission complete notice, another wave came at me. My guess is that the game didn't register the mission complete or otherwise just reset the area to add a new horde, I don't know...

Anyway, [b] I HIGHLY recommend playing the game of the hardest difficulty, master. [/b] Why? because the way difficulty works in this game is that it adjusts the amount of damage that bullets do across the board as opposed to messing with NPC stats. This means that at higher difficulties, you are more vulnerable, but enemies are easier to kill. Weird, right?

[h2] Survival [/h2]

This game includes several survival mechanisms. You have to eat occasionally, you have to keep your radiation exposure down, your guns tend to jam in the middle of firefights, and you have a depleting fatigue bar. While you have a ton of inventory space, your character can only carry 50kg. If you go over this limit, you can still walk and run around, however your fatigue bar will deplete faster and once its depleted, your character becomes momentarily immobile. This is terribly annoying, especially because the distances you have to walk are vast and due to this mechanic, you simply can't sprint from point A to point B, you have to take your time.

[h2] The Mods [/h2]

Perhaps the worst anomalies in the game are the bugs. This game's code was scripted on a sheet of toilet paper. The game crashes for several random reasons. If you eat food directly out of a dead enemy's inventory instead of putting it into your first -- game crash. If an NPC spawns at the other end of the map with a disrupted code -- game crash. [b] I HIGHLY recommend getting the ZRP mod which updates the game and fixes some of these issues. [/b] There will still be issues with the mod, but at least the game will be somewhat playable. There are other mods as well that update graphics and completely overhaul the experience, so be sure to explore Nexus or simply google some STALKER mods.

[h2] The Verdict [/h2]

STALKER is a kind of curiosity. It's an early 2000s game that, despite its flaws and bugs, was undoubtedly a masterpiece for its time. Today, the game is somewhat dated when compared to newer games like Fallout that basically offer similar experiences in a more optimized and grander way. However, STALKER has a unique and unmistakable atmosphere that grips you from time to time. This game gets intense and the environment has a tendency to provide you with unexpected situations that almost seem like they're scripted, but are actually fully organic and random. 

It's a game worth checking out and definitely a game worth modding. At the core level, STALKER is an excellent FPS RPG that has a lot to offer. With a few mods installed, it can make for an epic experience and all at a fraction of the cost of a Bethesda title.

A Stalker is someone who ventures into the ecological disaster zone created by the fictional second explosion of the Chenobryl Nuclear Power Plant to recover artifacts that defy the laws of physics. I won't go into further details of the game, as I the mysteriousness of The Zone, and how to survive there are the most endearing features of the game.
It took me a long, long time to fall in love with S.T.A.L.K.E.R. I first booted this game up on release day, and my good 'ol Athlon64X2 choked on it. Performance won't be a problem in this day and age, but the X-ray engine's poor optimization was killer back in '07, and the fact that the patches would erase your save game only added insult to injury (again, this won't affect the gamers of today). After I had finally tweaked the game into a playable state, I found an intriguing title with a fantastic premise, and a living, breathing world overflowing with atmosphere. However, exploring The Zone wasn't the beautiful experience that it should have been. The place was crawling with bugs, glitches and anomalies (and not just kind you are supposed to be exploring there!) The shooting physics were far from consistent, the translations were poor, and the game would still crawl along at a snail's pace. There is still much to love about the game, but playing through on vanilla left me feeling that the title just didn't live up to all that it could have been.
That all changed with I discovered the heavy modding scene for the series. I recommend reading up on the various fan overhauls for Stalker, and installing one before you even first step foot in The Zone. There are many to choose from, such as Complete 2009, Misery, or my personal favorite, Lurk. After playing through the game with fan enhancements, I found myself beyond taken by this title's bleak wonders. I would go as far as saying that Stalker with the Lurk mod is my favorite first person shooter experience of all time. I found myself so infatuated by the Zone and her mysteries, that I read  and enjoyed the book ('Roadside Picnic,' Arkady and Boris Strugatsky, 1971) and  watched and adored the film ('Stalker', by Andrei Tarkovsky, 1979). I also researched the fascinating tragedy of the real life Chernobyl disaster of 1986.
In conclusion, if you are a patient gamer who fancies a real challenge and getting lost in a bleak world in a devastated Ukrane, I simply can't recommend a modded version of S.T.A.L.K.E.R enough.
Get out of here, Stalker.

This game is rough. 
In the past I tried it out a couple of times, but as usual I dropped it after a few hours, unable to actually understand / focus on what I was doing and ultimately immerse myself in the game's ecosystem. And I need to reiterate that this game is rough. It will fist you, repeatedly. It will force you to abuse those F6 and F7 buttons until they'll be worn out.

This time though I was determined, so I prepared myself with a bit of lore beforehand, and also a quick research on how to modernize the game a bit with mods. I actually used the “starter pack” mod and a couple of high resolution texture packs, in order to keep the gameplay as vanilla as possible but at the same time avoid some headaches. 
And so, after some quick prepping I dove in head first and I pretty much straight up completed the game's main story and some side quests. And I loved it.

Don't get me wrong, the game is extremely janky, it didn't age very well, but if you're even a little bit interested in the lore you won't be disappointed. It actually takes inspiration from the book “Roadside Picnic”, and in some aspects it's quite similar to that, the main difference being there is no alien intervention in the game events. 

In short, we will be exploring the Chernobyl exclusion zone as a stalker who is affected by amnesia and is trying to recollect anything about himself and his past. The zone was contaminated by two nuclear disasters and aside from the radiation it has generated mutants, anomalies and special artifacts which have some powers and are really sought after by stalkers who sell them for profit.

At the time of this review I just completed the main story (unfortunately I found out afterwards that there are multiple ending possibilities, and the most common one will happen if you have a certain amount of money). The story though is just a means to get us moving forward, but it doesn't provide much lore about the world and its characters. In fact most of the information is scattered around the large semi open world hubs, in the form of PDAs, side quests and visual storytelling. I realize that completing the main quest I just barely scratched the surface of what this experience has to offer. 

What makes this game special for me, however, is the atmosphere which is conveyed. Despite the technical limitations of its time and overall jankiness, Shadow of Chernobyl really shines at immersing us in its world, offering lots of possibilities, areas to explore in order to look for precious artifacts and stashes hidden around. Every location, even if a bit empty, feels handcrafted and has a lot of personality. I really loved exploring underground bunkers where weird experiments took place, abandoned buildings and occupied military bases. Everything has an Eastern European feeling which really fascinates me and actually enhances the overall environment. Every location has some story to tell, if you are patient and curious enough to find out. 

This game oozes with lore. I actually found myself so fascinated by it that I turned a blind eye to the technical issues that plague it. The most annoying ones in my opinion are the somewhat frequent frame drops or freezes. It's amazing how some 17 years later SoC still struggles maintaining a consistent frame rate on any PC (I guess that won't ever be fixed), even though I must say that I had no problem during combat or tense situations, since those issues mostly presented themselves while traversing areas and moving around.

This review was really difficult to write because SoC is such a weird title. It has a unique setting, and it's kind of niche, so it's difficult to recommend it to everyone. Most people will probably be put off by the dated graphic presentation, or by the difficulty. But if you can get past the roughness of this game I'm pretty sure you won't be disappointed. Recommended!

Introduction:
S.T.A.L.K.E.R Shadow of Chernobyl is an open world survival (kinda horror) fps game where you are a STALKER, someone who is illegally residing in an area called the zone. The zone is a area that was created by a second Chernobyl disaster, it has alien like artifacts and mutants and is almost alive with its anomalies which are lethal. 

Review:
STALKER (and this goes for all 3 games) is very janky, glitches galore, screwed AI, meme lines, a weird translation, broken engine, and a lot more. However despite all this the game is still one of my favorites, still to this day this game has the best atmosphere of any game ever made I mean it and I played the hell out of silent hill 1-4. It's hard to explain without seeing for yourself just all the sounds the distant gunfire the ambient noise you hear in the labs  it all comes together in a immersive experience that I won't forget. The game has a host of various Russian weapons all feeling impactful except the starting pistol which unless you're playing clear sky is like using harsh language to try and kill people. STALKER uses a tactical shooting system where you and your enemies can die both easily, but the difficulties are kinda poorly balanced the myth on enemies becoming bullet sponges on the easy settings is not true. However you should stick to master in my opinion it's how the game is meant to be played you and your enemies both deal a lot of damage and the game rewards you enough to feel satisfying. The world is not a open world in a traditional sense its broken up into decently sized segments with specific factions in them or towns, some people might not like this and find it strange but honestly I'm so god damn fed up with open world games being this bland mish mash of hills and hundreds of locations filled with nothing. STALKER makes every location memorable even if it is some farm house it draws you in with all its atmosphere, quest in STALKER are more like jobs where you go out and kill something or someone or retrieve an item. This does not have leveling up so you only get items that can help you on your play through or a faction might like you slightly more, then there are artifacts. Artifacts are found usually by anomalies you either sell or attach them onto your belt for a bonus and a negative, they sell for a lot like even the ones that just plain suck are good for quick cash. STALKER to this day remains of the most genuinely haunting games I have ever played anyone who has had to travel at night or been through any of the labs already knows what I'm talking about. This game is subtle the sounds keep you on edge at all times, like whats behind that wall as the game has this ambiance in the background it just works so damn well at drawing the player in. As for how it holds up graphically it's beautiful things like textures are as good as some games coming out today, the sky boxes are lush and realistic, and especially the environment all dreary and cold looking as I said before it draws you in, but the npcs really don't hold up as well some of the lip syncing is hilariously bad, but you mostly will be alone in this game.

Final Note:
In the end I would highly recommend this game for all the reasons I listed even the jank its that charming. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is one of those special games that punches way above its weight class. It seeks to be an open-world, open-ended FPS/RPG with fluid relations between characters, emergent behavior in the wilds, and a compelling story and setting underpinning the whole thing. Those are lofty goals for any game, much less one from unproven developers back in 2007. What's shocking, then, is just how much it gets right even by modern standards.

In the world of S.T.A.L.K.E.R., the Chernobyl disaster spiraled outward to create the Zone, a harsh land ruled by mutated creatures, spatial anomalies, and mercenaries seeking to capitalize on the chaos. You play one such S.T.A.L.K.E.R. sans memories, sent back into the Zone to kill a mysterious figure close to the epicenter of it all. Along the way you'll forge alliances with other wanderers, discover threats far worse than mutated wildlife, and maybe come face to face with the source of the disaster itself. I wouldn't bank on that last one without some serious effort, though.

Instead of discreet levels, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is made up of maps that connect to form one contiguous world. Starting near the border of the Zone, you'll journey through radioactive swamps, underground bunkers, ghost towns, and more as you complete jobs for the other inhabitants. Sometimes that'll mean finding a stash of bizarre artifacts, and other times it'll mean gunning down a band of killers in their hideout. There's plenty to do in the Zone even without a specific mission, as you can loot corpses, hunt hidden stashes, and locate artifacts by navigating the treacherous anomalies that can crush, shock, or maim you with little warning.

All of this is accomplished from a first-person perspective, but don't expect the run-and-gun action of... anything, really. The combat in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is very much its own thing, a perpetually harrowing affair of dancing around cover, emptying magazines to only land one shot, and pumping dozens of bullets into charging beasts. Weapons in the Zone are inaccurate, difficult to use, and seemingly do no damage until you land a headshot that kills in an instant. I imagine it's more like real-world firefights than anyone would admit, but that doesn't necessarily make it fun to be eaten alive by wild dogs who dodged or shrugged off a dozen rounds.

You'll want to avoid combat as much as possible, at least at first, and luckily there's a robust and effective stealth system to make use of. This system tracks your light level, posture, noises made, and even gives you bolts you can toss to cause distractions (or trigger anomalies). There's a pretty big emphasis on stats across the board, really. Your character has resistances to all kinds of injury as well as a radiation level to monitor, your inventory has weight and conditions to consider, and every single NPC in the game has a reputation rating with you. There aren't always systems that address these stats directly, but they do represent significant depth to the simulation.

Attention to detail extends to the environments, and it is here that you'll find S.T.A.L.K.E.R.'s greatest strength. For a nearly ten-year-old game, the Zone looks amazing, with crumbling buildings and thick underbrush and rolling clouds blotting out the sun. There's a palpable sense of decay and instability wherever you go, and it only grows more intense as you approach the heart of the Zone. Every dark corner can hide a creature that wants your blood or an anomaly that can rend you in an instant, demanding caution and tense attention even in the daylight hours. And don't get me started on the underground bunkers... some of the most effective horror encounters I've experienced in gaming have come in the subterranean halls of the Zone.

I've spent a lot of time extolling the virtues of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. because they are many, but not without a price. It is an ambitious indie game after all, and that means all sorts of potential glitches and instability whenever you load in. Sometimes the AI breaks down, sometimes items vanish from the ground, and sometimes the thing will just crash when you least expect it. Beyond that there are definitely balance issues with the weapons and combat, exacerbated by missions with no real difficulty curve to them that might send you into a hostile mercenary camp before you find anything more formidable than a sawed-off. The rough translated text might actually be the worst offender, hiding key information and names behind English one step above Google Translate in some cases.

The Zone is a harsh and unforgiving place, and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. exemplifies it right down to the code. It's going to take you a long time and multiple tries to acclimate to its unique style, and turning to modding isn't a bad idea if the base game is just too daunting or janky. But once you come to grips with the combat and start learning the many ways to die in the Zone, you're in for one hell of a ride. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. does immersion and atmosphere better than almost any FPS, presenting you with a rich, frightening, living world that will fight you every step of the way.

I love this game even with all its faults. However this game needs a WARNING sign to all who want to try it. I will briefly mention what i love about the game then i will explain all the issues this game has in order to provide said warning label.

This game has a cult following and somewhat of a pedigree. The buggy nature of the game mixed with some interesting story and setting along with great atmosphere and weird slavic shenanigans make this a one of a kind experience, especially since nothing has come out since the last game quite like it. Yes i adore the Metro series but that series has a better story, its more focused and linear and provides better atmosphere imho, while on the other hand this series is more focused on the setting and is more like an RPG with a focus not on levels of the character but guns, armor and artifacts. So it's a more technical RPG. That is unique. Add to that an abundance of mods that provide such an experience that will give you hours and hours of replayability and challenge (think Escape from Tarkov but singleplayer).

Now for the negative aspects of the game but only Vanilla (no Mods):
As mentioned the game has A LOT of bugs. Game breaks easilly, enemies shoot at you without looking at you, reloading a save sometimes doesn't reset enemy knowledge of your location, getting spotted a mile away, they shoot you trought walls, objective markers dont dissapear, voices repeating same lines over and over again, enemies don't flinch, instadeath, clones spawn in a single spot, enemies spawn and aim at walls or at the sky until you shoot at them, they shoot at you even if there is no way they can see you..... the list goes on.

Whatever everyone is saying, NO the weapons don't deal more damage on higher difficulties towards enemies. The first weapons are inaccurate so that makes you think you are shooting blanks while you are actually missing shots. Headshots usually kill in one shot, but for some reason not always (armored enemies or just glitches). 

Most quests are fetch and kill quests and don't bother doing them unless you really want to. Most of the resources (and money) are easy to come by during the later half of the game. The progression is natural from bad weapons to not knowing which one to carry since there are a lot of good ones suddenly.

The bad part of the game is the way you traverse around the map while collecting stuff and completing missions only to have to walk back the entire way just to complete it for the reward. Along the way most enemies respawn or raids occur so because of the way the semi-open world is structured you will have linear corridors you have to pass and they are almost always garded at some point by either mutants, dogs, bandits or zombified enemies.

The game shines during the middle segment but falls flat when nearing the end (last 3 missions). It becomes very linear and you have a point of no return that the game doesn't mention but some characters do in some sort of way if you pay attention. The problem is that you have to be well prepaired to even have the possibility of succeding. These last missions are VERY poorly designed and ruin what the first half of the game established. The game doesn't have a combat focus at all, that is the reason everything is so innacurate and wonky. Then the game decides to throw 30+ enemies in a single building at you just at the end of a mission... and then there is almost a constant wave of enemies until the end of the game. You will HAVE TO kill most of them to be able to pass alive. They will instakill you around corners, nade you while in cover, snipe you with a gauss rifle from a building far out of normal range (for a normal chance to hit them because of the bad accuracy) or RPG you from across the map. The enemy placement is really really bad during the last bit of the game. SAVE OFTEN and plan ahead. F6 is your best friend!

The last bad thing is the story kind of. Yes the atmosphere is good but ruined during the last bit of the game cause of the abominable combat. Same goes for the story. But it also suffers from bad explanation. You have 0 developed characters other than the main character somewhat - the guy you are playing as. So any plot twist is not really surprising. There are 7 endings 5 of which are "fake" endings and 2 are "true" (1 of which is cannon ofc, like in Metro). The 5 fake ones are not that big of a deal and make no sense until you see the requirements to get all 5. The other 2 endings are a lot better but their explanation is really bad. I understand the concept cause I read about it more but for most people it will be confusing and won't give you much fulfillment (No catharsis).


With all that said I do really like the game. Just make sure to remember this is a unique game with a lot of problems and a lot of good things. The mod support is astonishing and after trying the base game mods should be on your list to install if you found the game to be interesting but could use a bit of tweaking.

I'm always reminded how amazing STALKER is every time I play it. This game is a prime example of a design philosophy that takes the focus off of catering to the player and places it into creating a tangible, living, breathing, dynamic world, to then drop them into it. Many games model and structure themselves around the player through scripting and triggered events. While the illusion convinces, it's still an illusion.

With STALKER it isn't. It’s a world that genuinely exists and evolves without concern for the player at all. The Zone doesn’t give a single **** about you. Factions fight you, each other (even when you’re not on the same map), mutants, and stumbling into battles, ongoing or finished, that have nothing to do with you is common. Actions affect reputation which plays an integral part in forming allegiances and causing rivalries. It’s a constantly evolving dynamic playground that always surprises. Not only does STALKER have an exemplary core design philosophy of complete and total indifference and apathy towards the player, it affords them very satisfying fundamental game play mechanics to experience the world in that context. Exhilarating gun play complimented by a realistic ballistics model, highly competent (though not perfect) AI, good inventory management and a weight system which demands strategic consideration, an abundance of items and cool gear, phenomenal sound design, day/night and dynamic weather cycle....then mix all this up with an unparalleled sense of atmosphere, dread, isolation and top it off with an enjoyable story and STALKER is second to none.

I remember the first time I played this game I was more than a little underwhelmed, so much so that I only lasted a few hours and only came back to it years later. To anyone who's yet to play this, keep this in mind: STALKER certainly doesn’t start out strong and does not give a very good first impression. The early weapons are terrible and don’t feel satisfying, the initial enemy encounters are hard and unrewarding, you can’t really go anywhere without being slaughtered, and the narrative is bland given the premise. Bugs (which were numerous on release) don’t help either. But once you get an assualt rifle with a scope so you can engage enemies at a distance, find some halfway decent gear to explore better, and (most importantly) start to understand how you’re in a world that you occupy but are not the reason of its existence, the game blossoms and there is really no other experience in gaming like it. STALKER is, plainly put, simply a brilliant testament to exemplary game design. That it’s lasted so long, is so loved, and still has a passionate modding community supporting it to this day is indicative of such. Unfortunately, the vanilla game remains an unpolished gem so IMO, modding is a bit of a necessity and I believe it is something that should be experienced as such (yes, especially for first time players). The vanilla game, while granting an incredibly solid foundation, is feeling its age and is in need of a few tweaks to raise it to parity with modern standards, both visually and game play wise, to see it to its fullest potential.

Nevertheless, I've rarely seen a game with such a strong core to be built off of to realize it to that potential, and while perhaps I could understand it's not to everyone's taste, if anyone puts in a decent amount of time into it they at least should be able to recognize the brilliance of what it accomplishes in the design strength of marginalizing the importance of catering to the player's experience and instead pays much more accord to the world they inhabit to be able to enable it. That's what make STALKER so engrossing, and it's not been matched to this day. 

I can only hope STALKER 2's developers don't forget what makes the first game such a masterpiece. Just keep in mind. If you're a STALKER virgin, remember: the game is not tailored to you. It doesn't care about you. It is a world for you to explore in complete indifference. If you can approach it with that mindset, you'll find an experience like no other in gaming.

Good hunting, STALKER.

[i]NOTE: As I am reviewing the original product, and not various third-party mods, this review is based on a vanilla playthrough. Please keep that in mind, thank you.[/i]

+ Functional, user-friendly navigation and quest-mapping device
+ Artifacts add slight RPG-like stat combinations
+ Vast, detailed environments
+ Very, very strong sense of atmosphere pervading throughout
+ Boasts a large and active modding community (many mods do well to address some of the game's various pitfalls)
+ Equipment and weight limitations do much to force the optimization of one's gear, and make one choose what to discard and what to keep; this leaves the player feeling both challenged and rewarded as they acclimate to the concept
+ Ambient sounds are absolutely fantastic, and keep the player consistently unsettled
+ Weapon degredation adds to the challenge, and makes one keep an eye on their equipment
+ Manner of interaction with various game-world NPCs is largely determined by the player's actions throughout the adventure
+ The game's world and atmosphere compliments an intriguing plot; the story, itself, rewards inquisitiveness
+ Moderate variation in firearms
+ Absolute plethora of side-missions

- No fast-travel; this likely will not bother the realists out there, but I felt that there could have been a comfortable middle-ground implemented that would have kept everyone happy
- Lots and lots of bugs, some of which are quite problematic (again, most of these can be remedied via the modding community)
- Largely flat and uninspired voice-acting
- Malleable NPC relationships notwithstanding, the story is fairly (although not completely) linear
- No autosave function (except when entering new areas, but the environments are mostly sprawling areas, making this insufficient); massively frustrating when you die 45 minutes into a new area and forget to manually save, forcing you to take significant steps back in progress (although I believe there is a mod available to remedy this)

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl is the first STALKER game, but it takes place a year after its prequel, Clear Sky. You play as an amnesiac man named Marked One, who continues the last mission he remembered: hunt down a stalker named Strelok who managed to enter the center of the Zone, the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant. It's an open-world FPS-RPG where you collect items and do quests. Imagine Fallout mixed with Metro, set in a post-apocalyptic, post-Soviet country with bandits, mutants, and good ol' radiation. It has levels based on real locations, too, like the ghost town Pripyat.

Compared to its prequel which I played first, SoC is better in so many ways despite the prequel being the newer one. The early missions are simple and easy, welcoming to any new player. Money, armor, weapons, and artifacts are also very easy to find, you don't need to buy them from shop or go inside an anomaly as they are given as rewards or just laying around. Some unique, more powerful weapons and armor are available and easy to find. All of these combined makes the combat easier to handle, but still a bit dangerous. The final levels are sadly linear and has plenty of combat, but I didn't really find it difficult thanks to my gear.

However, those easy-to-find gear came with a consequence: money becomes almost useless. I always play scavenger in open-world games, and I don't ever need to use money as there are no overpowered gear that is only available at traders. There's also no fast travel, not even those paid guides, and you have to run back and forth to do some sidequests. Biggest flaw of the game. I only recommend doing the more unique ones, such as find armor/weapon or the "kill named person" assassination quests which yield good rewards and unique dialogue. Otherwise, the backtracking gets tedious and you only get generic lines and useless money.

This game has 7 endings, but you can only get 3 per playthrough. 1 is a "false" ending, which is short and unsatisfying, but depends on your actions during the game. The other 2 are the "true" endings. To get the true endings, you must do a series of short sidequests involving meeting people from your past, but other than that what you did doesn't really matter, unlike in the false ones. The bad ending is only a bit longer than the false ones, but happens in a different room. The good ending, and also the canon one, is quite longer and involves a lot of combat. But it's worth it, and it gives you a chance to try out your powerful end-game gear.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is a legendary trilogy about an alternative world where the Chernobyl explosion created a mysterious place called the Zone. In this review I’d like to tell you about the first part of this trilogy called S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl.

Plot:

In this game you play as the man called the “Marked One”. He was driven from Pripyat in a death truck together with other people but the truck got into an accident. A few hours after the accident someone found this truck as well as the “Marked One” who was still alive and took him to the trader called Sidorovich. At this moment the game begins.

Setting:

The Zone… The Zone is a beautiful place full of amazing destroyed buildings, forgotten transport and natural mutations… However, it is only one side of the coin, shiny and picturesque, but the other side of it is dark and rotten. Lots of mutated animals, cruel and ruthless, are rather dangerous residents of this place. The victims of the experiments have escaped from deep laboratories and now live in the darkest and most dangerous part of the Zone. But the most dangerous inhabitants of this place are not brainless mutants… These are people who are known as stalkers. Some of them are just adventurous people who want to find escapades… Most of them  die in a few hours or days after they cross the territory of the Zone… Most of the stalkers are bandits, thugs, deserters, killers and robbers who want to escape justice from the outside. Yesterday it was your brother in arms, today he stubs a knife in your back because of the artifact or money. “You can’t trust anyone in this cruel place” is the most important precept of the Zone and if you follow this rule, you maybe stay alive longer than one week…  To survive, people create different factions such as “Duty”, “Freedom” “Bandits” and so on. What’s more, you can earn a lot of money. You must find special stones called “Artifacts”.They’ve got special effects that affect people who wear them on their belt or in a backpack but most of them are radioactive. To find artifacts, you must find anomalies. These are special zones that have different effects upon the people. Most of them are dangerous and eventually fatal except space anomaly which teleports people who touch it.

Atmosphere and music:

These are two things why millions of people have loved and have been playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R. since the moment of its release. I’ll begin with the music. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. music is fascinating. The music depends on the location, weather and action, but it is always cool and atmospheric. As for the atmosphere, it’s the most mysterious and thrilling game ever for the CIS people. You can just sit near the fire in the rainy weather with other stalkers and listen to their stories while one of the stalkers will be playing the guitar. Besides, you can listen to jokes about the Zone. Even in this cruel, rotten and dark place, people tell jokes and stay happy… But sometimes stalkers tell you dark stories about their comrades who died in an anomaly or were eaten by mutants. However, the saddest stories are about novices who were killed by machineguns of military men near the entrance to the Zone or were torn to pieces in an anomaly. That’s a horrible sight. But the most terrifying scene is zombified stalkers. They are made by a psi-field. Not long ago they were ordinary stalkers and now they are brainless zombies, poor souls that are beyond help because the destructive process of their brain is irreversible. They still can use weapon and attack everyone. When you are killing them, you can hear them talk in their madness and it is grim and wistful… “Daughter, look how grown you are! Daddy is coming home soon…” said one zombified person before dying from my bullet. Some of them just wanted to escape from the Zone but they couldn’t do it: "The Zone...Zone is a bitch...I must get out of here..."

Gameplay:

It’s a first-person shooter survival horror game, but there are a lot of RPG elements. The player does not gain additional abilities or statistics like most RPGs (though the player does level through game play from "novice" to "expert" which has slight effects on the ability to aim accurately), but is instead allowed to attach artifacts which can increase or decrease player attributes. Artifacts found within the Zone have both positive and negative effects except for some rare artifacts which have only positive attributes.

Now, for a warning. This has to do with the end of the game but I will try my best to explain this with little/no spoilers for anything plot related, because I really, REALLY wish I had know this before I played the game:

the last two/three levels of this game are an awful experience. They are unfairly difficult in a way that is not possible to predict and prepare for without knowing ahead of time what you are getting into. I won't go into the context of what's happening or where it is happening, but suffice to say you're fighting an ASSLOAD of enemies that can easily one shot you in a setting that will kill you just by standing in it to long. It is INSANELY EASY TO SOFTLOCK yourself into not being able to complete the game (happened to me TWICE meaning I had to redo about 8 hours of the game for BS reasons). Here's what you need to avoid that:

- you need a powerful weapon with a LOT of ammo. These enemies will gut you as soon as they turn their attention on you; the best option is to take them out BEFORE they have the opportunity to fight back. That means precision head-shots with a quality weapon (mid-tier assault rifles aint gonna cut it, I'm afraid).
- You need VERY good armor. Like I said before, the enemies hit harder than a dump truck here. If you want to stand even the most remote of chances, you need some strong armor. More importantly though you need armor (and artifacts as well) that have good stats against radiation, which brings us to the last suggestion....
- you need a metric FUCKTON of anti-rad kits and medkits. This is non-negotiable. The radiation in the final area of the game is SO ridiculously extreme that it is, by far, your biggest enemy, and by far the single biggest culprit in the game for softlocking people out of completing it. Even after killing/escaping every hostile enemy in the final area, the radiation will continue to get worse and worse and if you do NOT have the right equipment to fight it literally all the way up to the final cutscene, there is a very real risk you will soft lock yourself literally FEET AWAY FROM TRIGGERING THE END. It is BEYOND frustrating. Make sure, for god's sake, that you take the radiation threat seriously at the end of the game. Up to that point, radiation has been at worst a moderate threat in game, which luls you into a false sense of security and might make you not collect enough anti-rad artifacts and equipment throughout. This is a MASSIVE MISTAKE to make. You absolutely need them for the final area, you will NOT SURVIVE if you do not prepare for this. 

There, that's all you need to know to keep yourself from soft-locking yourself out of the end of the game. So long as you heed my advice and keep these points in mind for the end of the game, you should be golden. It's such a shame that the game ends on such a bullshit and unfair note like that, because evreything leading up to it is truly remarkable. But nevertheless, even with the terrible last few hours of the game, the vast majority of the game is incredible and definitely worth your time. Pick it up whenever you can, and good hunting, Stalker.

STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl is slavjank at its finest. While the game has aged relatively well, one must still keep in mind that this is a game produced with shoestring budget and had a somewhat troubled development cycle. The caveats in mind, STALKER is an excellent semi-open world shooty-survival-y romp with a decent story to it. The story is told through a few cutscenes, but mostly through either someone radioning you and telling something has happened, or through a dialog box before or after a mission.

At its core, STALKER is a shooter leaning more into survival and methodical play, rather than fast paced action. In the Zone, a few shots can drop you, but the enemies follow similar rules. The only thing that gives the enemies any kind of advantage, is their numbers and their uncanny ability to throw grenades. The game does not really have a stealth system, but you can equip a silencer in your weapon and pick off a few enemies before the rest notice that something is amiss.

The game's age shows mostly through the slightly muddy visuals and many aged systems. For instance, you cannot repair your weapons or armor without the use of a mod that enables the functionality, which means you will be replacing your shooter and suit frequently. Thankfully(?), there are no upgrade systems either, so any suit A is going to be equivalent to any other suit A.

There are a number of things I would recommend you change if you are just getting into STALKER: firstly, I would suggest getting the Complete mod or something similar, as they fix a number of issues and bugs, and add some much-needed quality of life features, like repairing gear at Barkeep. Before that, you likely won't need to repair your items, as you will be rapidly acquiring better weapons and protective suits. After that, the rate of acquisitions slows down and you will find yourself sticking to one or two weapons and one suit for an extended period of time. In addition to the mod, you may want to look into tweak guides that allow you to get rid of the absolutely horrible headbobbing, and allows you to improve the visuals/performance of the game.

STALKER is definitely not for everyone, but for those whom this style of game appeals will love it, and revisit the Zone for years to come even in spite of the flaws and shortcomings of the currently released games. One can only wonder how STALKER 2 will be like. Keep your Quicksave button close at hand, and get out of here, STALKER.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl — a game that takes root in your mind.
Released back in 2007, it still manages to evoke emotions that modern titles rarely deliver.
The atmosphere is nothing short of phenomenal. The first time I stepped out of the bunker and heard a guitar playing by the campfire, I felt it — I was in a different world. Frightening, bleak, but strangely captivating. Everything here works toward immersion — the weather, the architecture, the abandoned machinery, strange anomalies, and the sounds that send shivers down your spine.
Gameplay isn’t about non-stop action. Survival comes first. Ammo is scarce, enemies don’t forgive mistakes, mutants are fast and terrifying, and a grenade can save you — or kill you. I genuinely feared for my character. As I moved forward, I caught myself thinking: “Just let me make it to the next camp…”
I loved how the game tells its story. No hour-long cutscenes — just fragments of information you piece together yourself. Who are you? What happened here? Why are you even in the Zone? The answers are there, but you have to earn them. And your choices actually matter — the ending depends on what you do. That’s what makes it so gripping.
Sound — the nervous system of the game.
Seriously, the sound design is one of the main characters. Distant howls, rustling in the bushes, sudden emissions, the crackle of a radio when you approach an anomaly… The sound isn’t just background — it’s part of the gameplay. And the music in the stalker camps? That’s the soul of the game.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl is an experience. Sometimes rough, sometimes unpolished (yes, bugs do happen), but absolutely unique. This game has a heart — and it beats with every step you take in the Zone.

Тут усе працює на занурення — погода, архітектура, покинута техніка, дивні аномалії та звуки, від яких мурашки по шкірі.

Мені сподобалося, як гра подає сюжет. Жодних годинних катсцен — лише шматочки інформації, які ти збираєш сам. Хто ти? Що тут сталося? Навіщо ти тут? Відповіді є, але їх потрібно заслужити. І від твоїх рішень залежить, яким буде фінал. Це справді чіпляє.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Shadow of Chernobyl is a cult classic for those who dig the Russian/Ukrainian aesthetics coupled with some minor RPG and survival elements. Visually the game can be dated looking and same applies to the feeling of the game with it's controls and UI. To many new stalkers the game might come off as very weird, unappealing, or boring to people who start out for the first time. The atmosphere and world has a slow way of drawing you in slowly until you're deep into the game and it's setting.

The setting and atmosphere is definitely the strongest thing this game has. You explore the outskirts of Pripyat and the notorious Chernobyl NPP after a strange second disaster happens and alters the world and defies both science and reality itself with Anomalies and artifacts. The world is fairly decent sized and split into sectors. You'll explore most of them multiple times. The underground labs are probably some of the most horrifying experiences I've had in a long time with the sound design and darkness. 

The gameplay is probably the weakest part of the whole experience. Guns have a tendency to be inconsistent but scoped weapons reign supreme due to how long range engagements can me along with seeing where your bullet went. Bodyshots are easily shrugged off by even lowly bandits so headshots are essentially a must to win. Mutants on the other hand are either weak or bullet sponges. The player character no matter what difficulty is weak. You might have to resort to abundant use of quicksaves and some save scumming since the game is fairly difficult in some sections.

The economy in this game is fairly brutal meaning you'll have to do some jobs and grinding by taking artifacts, loot, and risking your own life to make small amounts of cash only to save up and blow it all on buying that expensive ass new suit with exoskeleton support that looks awesome. Different traders offer different prices for specific items, such as the ecologist paying top dollar for any artifacts or mutant pieces you bring them. However everything has durability meaning when you purchase anything be ready to chuck it away or sell the broken gear for a mere fraction of what you payed for before. The game is also not very friendly to loot hoarders with bullets and all other things that go into your inventory taking up weight. The game punishes you for stocking up on too much gear (such as having like 1000 extra AK rounds) you do not need basically forcing you to take the bare essentials.

Now let me get into the artifacts. These are a staple of the game's experience and what really makes this game from shiny silver to absolute gold. Artifacts are found in stashes you find locations for or inside an anomaly which will instantly eviscerate your character. These things are high risk high reward and you can easily find them with the naked eye. Not all artifacts are good or sell for much. A number of them are pretty much junk artifacts that irradiate your character or offer very little benefit however when you find something like maybe 4 moonlight artifacts you can pretty much sprint infinitely even when you're carrying too much. Some items can effect different aspects of the gameplay such as stopping bleeding, increased resistances, increased health, and radiation removal. A lot of these do come with downsides such as emitting radiation, making you weaker to specific attacks, and overall increasing the bleed out rate.

The story in this game is basically next to non-existent. Like it's there but at the same time it's really nothing special. I know I said the gameplay is the weakest part but I think I take that back now. There are 2 main endings with the one having sub endings based on what you did and yes there is a true canon ending if you go out of your way to figure it out.

NO FAST TRAVEL. Expect to do some walking and rationing your gear alongside avoiding fights from point A to point B if you have to.

I'd say S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Shadow of Chernobyl is a must play game. It might not be for everyone but it is definitely one of the best for what it is. Also if I find someone who calls this game series Russian Fallout I will borderline hurt them.
