You play as a S.T.A.L.K.E.R. or scavenger and referred to as “the marked one” since you have the tattoo S.T.A.L.K.E.R. branded on your arm. You have lost your memory in a car crash and have been taken to a S.T.A.L.K.E.R. camp where you will carry out tasks to prove yourself to the rest of the camp. The camp is located in the middle of the “zone” which surrounds the nuclear power plant in Chernobyl, Ukraine, where a core meltdown occurred in 1986. In the game, the zone is filled with mutant dogs, radioactive anomalies and other creatures that are obstacles in your overall goal of learning about what the zone is and who you really are.

Gameplay:
The creators of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. had a unique vision for the interactive environment of the game. They wanted to create an atmosphere where you do not start at “level one” and work your way up, gradually upgrading weaponry, health, armor etc. They wanted to allow you to roam everywhere you want and retreat back to anywhere you want to go, creating the allusion of a non-linear storyline, though some areas are still blocked off until you accomplish some tasks. 

Although the view from your character’s perspective is most certainly a FPS, the game reacts and feels like a role-playing game. There are no limits or restrictions on where you can travel to or backtrack to. Your voiceless character is equipped with a PDA that keeps track of your missions, your map and your contacts. Your character also has a backpack to carry weapons, ammo, food and anything else you may come across during your journey through the zone. The weight of your backpack will either limit your ability to run great distances or restrict you to a few steps and sometimes it will be so heavy you cannot even move. The heavier your backpack is, the faster you will run out of breathe which is measured by the indicator in the bottom left of your screen. Depending on where you are in the game this will become a big factor if you are able to outrun enemies or become so exhausted you are standing still. Be careful how many weapons you carry.
As you travel to complete missions, you will notice the strange anomalies, which look like either swirling electric tornadoes, lightning strikes and flashes of light. Some of these anomalies will produce artifacts that can be traded for other items or even equipment. The artifacts will add either positive or negative affects to your characters ability to resist fire, radiation, electricity or chemical burns. The Slug artifact helps your nourishment, drive out radiation and improve blood coagulation, but decreases your character’s defense in electric, thermal and chemicals damage.

As you begin playing the game you will quickly realize there are no real checkpoints and discover one of the most annoying aspects of the game - you need to either manually save your game yourself or continue to hit the quicksave key every few seconds because YOU DIE SO FRIGGIN MUCH. Getting hit with one bullet may put you down, and if it does not happen to kill you instantly, you will either get exhausted to the point where you cannot move and get attacked again or you will bleed to death because you forgot to use bandages.

Your weaponry will depend on how well you scout out an area or how well you can trade. Depending on where you search or who you kill you could find the best weapon in the game right away by searching the body of a dead militant. Most of the items you acquire will be found on dead bodies and will range from energy drinks for increasing stamina, bandages to stop bleeding, med kits and food to increase health, and ammo and guns to kick ass with. Guns range from sawed off shotguns, to assault rifles to silenced handguns. Gun fights feel very realistic, as your enemies will try and duck and cover behind trees, bushes and debris to fire back and sometimes your gun will jam forcing you reload. But gunfights are not always as fun as they first seem. The AI will react incredibly lifelike at some points; if you are getting shot at by a militant with a shotgun that only has two shots, after the second shot is fired the enemy will run for cover to reload. But there is a point where I wiped out six or seven enemies because they all were staring straight up into the sky. The rest of the enemies did not even fire back even after their friends were dying. There was also a point where one of my saved games took me where I could not move nor could I change weapons.

The mutants are probably the spookiest aspect of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. There are dozens of different weird looking monsters that will surprise the hell out of you when you least expect it. One mutant can make himself invisible and do massive amounts of damage to you when you try and locate where he actually is. Another mutant can do a series of telekinetic attacks that will cause your vision to become very blurry and dizzy. The telekinetic mutant is extremely scary as you have no idea what to expect from a walking unarmed zombie-looking monster.

Graphics and Sound:
First glances will label S.T.A.L.K.E.R. as an “okay” looking game, but the more you play the more you realize how incredibly awesome the game looks and feels as successfully simulates the feel of a desolate, abandoned countryside. The wind blows and chucks up clouds of dust while at the same time causing the grass and trees to sway back and forth in sync. As impressive as that is, the real-time interactions are far more impressive than that. Hundreds of birds, dogs and boars roam the planet, each with their own ambient noise if you happen by the outskirts of their territory. The game looks and feels real.

If you refer back to my Half-Life 2 review, I mentioned how the time of day changes as your progress through the game. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. takes this a step further where day becomes dusk, dusk becomes night, and night becomes dawn over the course of your journey. You will notice the sky is impressively realistic and sometimes an area becomes so dark you will need to use your flashlight or night vision to see. At some points of the game it will even begin to rain and flashes of lighting will be followed a few seconds later by booms of thunder. The flashlight in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is best similar to and just as useful as the one in Doom, only this time you can have your flashlight out with your weapons.

There are tons of ambient noises in the game, some recognizable and some so spooky you will not want to venture further into the abandoned building. Walking over different terrain will change your footsteps and if you are trying to sneak up on an enemy, it would be best to walk for they will hear you coming if you are running behind them. Walking through trees and shrubbery will also cause noise.

Though some characters speak English in the game, most of them speak Ukrainian or Russian. It is very difficult to understand most of what other characters in the game are saying so you may need to resort to body language. If a STALKER is holding a gun to you, and using his other hand making a downward motion, it is recommended you to holster your weapon.

Bottom Line: Replaying this after 10 years, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is indeed one for the books. It has the most involved sense of dread and ominous tones, which is well deserved given its storyline. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. as taken FPS to the next level offering impressive real-time graphics (that still hold up), a game that can be completed in thousands of different ways and a very spooky theme. Though still bug riddled, it’s definitely worth playing.

I rarely ever write a review, but for this one I felt obligated to do so. Simply put, this entered to my list of "one of the best games I've ever played".

S.T.A.L.K.E.R: Shadow of Chernobyl is an amazing game and, more than that, an unique experience. It's the most atmospheric game I've played to date and, even though it's relatively old, the gameplay feels great and the combat is tactical and rewarding.

Although I already knew that the game had a great atmosphere and combat, what really surprised me is the history... because I wasn't expecting to be this GOOD. It takes some time to pick up but, when it does, you can't stop playing. The plot develops in such a way that you just want to play until the very end, all day everyday, just to know what will happen next.

Speaking of when, the game really "clicked" for me in Lake Yantar (which is the first half part of the game), not only because of the plot at this point, but especially because of the place. Lake Yantar is very different from other places of the game: it's eerie and mysterious but at the same time very calming. I liked everything about it, including the color palette and ambient soundtrack. I consider it my favorite place in the zone, along with Cordon.

Not to say that the game wasn't enjoyable since the very beginning, but this part is definitely one of my favorites, and from there on the game is a never-ending climax.

Special mention goes also for the labs, the most memorable parts of the game... a mixed feeling of "I want to go there and discover the mysteries but I'm too scared to do that". They explain everything that happened inside it without saying a word, and it's easily the scariest places of the zone.

As a negative, the game does feels dated and unpolished in some ways given the release date and the problems it had in the development phase but... all in all, they're minor issues that don't take away the experience as a whole.

And here is my recommendation to all new stalkers, based on my personal experience: don't play with Complete! Or, at least, play the vanilla game for the first few hours and then try Complete, just to compare both side by side. I bet that you will prefer vanilla.

I played the vanilla game initially and decided to try Complete after because of the graphical improvements and, although it does look good and more polished, the game goes from being very challenging to a walk in the park. The tweak to the visual distance of enemies killed the game for me because a simple change like that dumbed down the enemies completely.

That isn't the only thing that the mod changes for the sake of being easier, but it's certainly the most significant one - and the difficult is one of the things that makes this game be what it's.

Now that you've read it, hand over your artifacts or you're dead!
